Tanker market outlook for 2026
In the fourth part of our shipping market outlook series we are focusing on the tanker sector with Maritime Strategies International (MSI) Analyst Tim Smith.
Speaking to the Seatrade Maritime Podcast Smith says that the tanker sector is coming into 2026 on a very strong footing.
A look back at 2025
The end of 2025 has set the tanker market up strongly as it went into 2026. “The tanker sector comes into 2026 on a very strong footing. And also, of course we are seeing those geopolitical elements, that kind of turbulence continue with, US actions in and around Venezuela, through December and of course into January 2026,” Smith says.
Looking the geopolitical situation from a purely tanker market perspective Smith says: “These typically tend to be positive elements in driving up of course uncertainty, energy security and tanker earnings when we see more and more geopolitical turmoil.” This layers on top of an expected positive picture in terms of trade volumes buoyed by
production increases.
Related: US diesel export ban wouldn’t play out as Trump Administration expects
The potential negative of high production is that it is outstripping relatively subdued oil demand growth.
“We're seeing that buildup of stockpiling as well in 2026 that potentially has some pitfalls for the market for the tanker sector later on if conditions become over, supplied and we start to see a pullback in production,” Smith explains.

GULF OF OMAN — The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) center issued Warning 120-26 after the master of an oil tanker reported the ship struck by an unknown projectile 9 nautical miles (10 miles, 17 kilometers) northeast of Ash Shishah, Oman.
UKMTO logged the report at 8:25 p.m. UTC on August 24 and classified the event as an attack. The master said the projectile damaged the engine room and left the tanker unable to proceed. UKMTO said the crew was reported safe and that environmental impact was unknown in the initial warning.
The stated position sits on the eastern face of Oman’s Musandam Peninsula, on the Gulf of Oman approach to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC), in an advisory issued August 23 with information current to 3:00 p.m. UTC that day, rated the strait SEVERE and recorded no confirmed attacks in the prior 48 hours.
Warning 120-26 is the first UKMTO attack product on that corridor after that cutoff.
In a separate incident the same calendar day, UKMTO Warning 119-26 said a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile 63 nautical miles (72 miles, 117 kilometers) west of Yanbu, Saudi Arabia, with a fire on the main deck.
That event is in the Red Sea, not the Gulf of Oman.

Fleet managers have also dispatched refined product tankers toward the Middle East in anticipation of regional refineries needing to clear inventories built up during the conflict before they can restart production.
In effect, the market is pricing a volatile mix of constrained supply, elevated risk and anticipated access.
Beyond the Gulf, the partial reopening is beginning to reshape global trade patterns that were radically altered by the disruption.
With Hormuz traffic severely restricted, oil flows were forced onto longer routes, including voyages around the Cape of Good Hope that significantly increased shipping distances and costs.
Those diversions pushed up ton-mile demand — a key measure of shipping activity — with distances on some trades nearly tripling as vessels avoided the chokepoint, according to shipping analyst reports.
Early signs suggest that these crisis-era patterns may start to unwind as Gulf exports gradually resume.
But for now, alternative routing remains in use, reflecting persistent uncertainty over access through Hormuz itself.
A CONFIDENCE PLAY
Ultimately, the constraint facing the tanker market is no longer purely physical. It is psychological and financial.

While critical mineral markets differ from oil markets, strategic stockpiles can still provide an important emergency buffer, helping safeguard industrial activities during supply shocks.
The conflict in the Middle East has provided another stark reminder of the vulnerabilities affecting mineral supply chains. While the key impacts of the conflict centred on oil and gas markets, there has also been considerable impact on mineral and metal markets from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, notably for aluminium, sulphur and helium.
The Middle East accounts for around 8% of global aluminium production, and production curtailments at several regional smelters added strain to an already tight market. The Defense Department on Monday announced framework agreements with Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin aimed at expanding production of critical Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, interceptor components as the military seeks to replenish missile inventories through expanded, long-term production capacity.
The agreements come as demand for Patriot and THAAD interceptors has increased following conflicts in Iran and Ukraine that strained U.S. missile inventories .
They also come days after a Center for Strategic and International Studies analysis estimated the United States had depleted roughly two-thirds of its pre-war Patriot interceptor inventory during the conflict with Iran.
Defense officials said the agreements are intended to support the department’s long-term procurement objective of nearly 14,000 Patriot and THAAD interceptors by providing sustained demand signals to critical suppliers throughout the defense industrial base.
The initiative is designed to triple production capacity for Patriot Advanced Capability-3, or PAC-3, Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors and quadruple production capacity for THAAD interceptors.

Summary
Refinancing risk in private credit appears increasingly differentiated. While the aggregate contractual maturity schedule is extended and most analysed positions continue to be reported at fair value close to cost, valuation pressure is concentrated within a smaller subset of borrowers approaching maturity.
Between conventional refinancing and default sits a broad spectrum of outcomes including higher-cost refinancing, amend-and-extend transactions, covenant modifications, sponsor support and liability management exercises.
As a result, the future trajectory of private credit may depend less on the volume of debt maturing and more on how lenders, sponsors and borrowers respond as those maturities approach.
For investors, the key challenge is therefore not identifying whether a maturity wall exists. It is determining which borrowers can successfully navigate it.

The Army is investing billions of dollars to bring nuclear power to military bases, selecting five companies to build nuclear microreactors at installations across the U.S., the service announced Wednesday in collaboration with the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit.
The service said it expects to field more than 20 microreactors across Department of Defense installations.
